article.title: trumps american history
article.author: Eva Amar
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I have a confession to make, and I'm not particularly proud of it. Somewhere between middle school and high school, I decided history wasn't for me. It seemed like an endless parade of dates, timelines, and wars, interrupted by still more wars. I paid enough attention to pass the tests, but I certainly wasn't sitting on the edge of my seat waiting to find out what happened next. What did any of that have to do with my life? Well, seventy years of living have given me a rather different perspective. History isn't simply a collection of dates, wars, and presidents. It's our baseline. Without it, how can we recognize the warning signs of something we've already lived through? This year America celebrates its 250th birthday. Compared with civilizations whose histories stretch back thousands of years, we're practically adolescents. We've packed extraordinary wrongdoing into those two and a half centuries, but we've also advanced science, medicine, education, and human rights, helped defeat tyranny abroad, and produced generations willing to challenge injustice at home. We have much to celebrate. And much to answer for. We began by taking land from the people who were already here. Native Americans were displaced through conquest, broken treaties, forced removals, and massacres. We declared that all men were created equal while allowing human beings to be bought and sold as property. Related: He said. He said. End of Story. Then came the Mexican–American War of 1846–1848, which ended with Mexico losing approximately 55 percent of its territory. California, where I live, was once part of Mexico, along with much of the Southwest. Which brings to mind something Mexican Americans have been saying for generations: “We didn't cross the border. The border crossed us.” For some families, their ancestors lived here before the border moved. We abolished slavery but subjected Black Americans to generations of segregation. We denied women the vote, excluded Chinese immigrants by law, and permitted forced sterilization under eugenics programs. In 1939, the United States turned away the St. Louis, carrying 937 passengers, most of them Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi persecution. The passengers returned to Europe, where several countries accepted them; ultimately, 254 were murdered in the Holocaust. Only three years later, our government began incarcerating approximately 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, most of them American citizens. During the McCarthy era, accusations of communist sympathies could amount to professional and social death sentences, destroying careers and reputations on little more than suspicion. Our government surveilled civil rights leaders, including Martin Luther King Jr., while gay Americans endured generations of discrimination. Yet Americans also fought to correct injustices. The Civil Rights Act became law in 1964. Marriage equality became the law of the land in 2015. And in 2022, the Supreme Court overturned nearly fifty years of constitutional protection for a woman's right to decide whether to terminate a pregnancy she cannot, for whatever reason, carry to term. I'm not asking anyone to inherit the guilt of previous generations. I'm asking us to inherit their lessons. Facts Are Stubborn Things In 1770, John Adams, defending British soldiers accused in the Boston Massacre, reminded a courtroom that “facts are stubborn things.” More than 250 years later, those words deserve another hearing. On January 29, 2025, the president signed Ending Radical Indoctrination in K–12 Schooling. The executive order directs federal agencies to develop strategies addressing what it calls indoctrination, including through federal funding, and reestablishes the President's Advisory 1776 Commission. The administration says it wants patriotic education, parental rights, and an end to teaching children that they are personally responsible for historical injustices. Children shouldn't carry the guilt of previous generations. But there's a difference between assigning blame for slavery and teaching children how slavery worked, whom it harmed, and why Americans fought to end it. The order does not itself ban teaching slavery or segregation. But its definitions and funding provisions raise the question of whether teachers may feel discouraged from examining uncomfortable history honestly. On March 27, 2025, the president signed a second order: Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History. This one extends to the Smithsonian and federal historical sites, directing officials to address presentations the administration considers divisive or improperly disparaging. The administration says it is restoring accuracy and celebrating American achievement. Historians and preservation advocates worry about political influence over what the public is allowed to see. At the President's House in Philadelphia, which served as the presidential residence for George Washington and John Adams before the White House was built in Washington, D.C., the National Park Service removed exhibits documenting the lives of people enslaved by Washington in January 2026. Philadelphia sued, and a federal appeals court subsequently cleared the way for the administration to replace the original displays. Washington helped establish a republic dedicated to liberty, and he enslaved human beings. Both are true. Why should knowing one require concealing the other? And what about the Smithsonian, where generations have gone to discover their country's story? Should the exhibits change according to what each administration finds flattering? History isn't a public relations campaign. Nor should the free press become one: its job is to examine the record, not repeat an administration's preferred version. It's optics. Pure optics. The Lessons We Keep Encountering History doesn't stay neatly tucked away in textbooks or museum exhibits. It has a way of rearing its head in the morning news, sometimes in ways that are uncomfortably familiar. Take immigration, for example. Undocumented immigrants harvest our food, clean our hotels, care for our elderly, and build our homes. Many have raised American-born children. According to the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy, undocumented immigrants paid an estimated $96.7 billion in federal, state, and local taxes in 2022, including $25.7 billion toward Social Security and $6.4 billion toward Medicare. A country has the right to enforce its immigration laws. But surely there's a distinction between someone who poses a genuine danger and someone whose principal violation is entering without authorization or overstaying a visa. Instead, we're seeing immigration operations involving officers with covered faces, sometimes without visible identifying information. Questions about detention conditions, oversight, and the use of force deserve answers. And then there are the children. Related: Stay Woke: What My Father Learned About Race in America A child waiting outside school for a mother who never arrives. A little boy watching the clock, wondering why his father hasn't come home from work. Many children affected by immigration enforcement are American citizens. They have broken no law, yet may suffer devastating consequences when a parent is detained. The St. Louis and the Japanese American families forced from their homes belong to different historical circumstances. But isn't recognizing both the differences and the unsettling echoes part of why we study history? And Then There Is the Rest of the World And history doesn't stop at our borders. It follows us into the relationships we've built with other nations, the promises we've made, and the alliances we've come to depend upon. For generations, America helped build alliances with Canada, Britain, France, Germany, and other democracies. We stood beside them through wars and crises, and they stood beside us. After September 11, 2001, NATO invoked Article 5, its collective-defense provision, for the first and only time in its history. It was invoked in defense of the United States. Now some of our closest allies are preparing to rely less on us. They haven't abandoned America, but they're building arrangements that may no longer depend on our participation. Then there are questions about our own use of military force. In September 2025, the United States military attacked a boat in the Caribbean suspected of carrying drug traffickers. Two men survived the first strike and clung to the wreckage. A second strike killed them. The administration defended the operation as lawful. But whatever those men were suspected of doing, suspicion is not conviction. They were clinging to the wreckage when the second strike came. For generations, ours was a country others often turned to for help. We weren't always right, and we never accomplished those things alone. But now I wonder who will be there to pick us up if we fall. The People on the Beam There's a famous 1932 photograph of eleven construction workers eating lunch on a steel beam suspended hundreds of feet above Manhattan. Their feet dangle over the city. They smoke, talk, and eat as though sitting on a park bench. Now imagine that photograph with a different cast of characters: a grandmother clutching her grandchild, a father holding an infant, teenagers, working mothers, retirees. Ordinary Americans, sitting together with no visible safety net beneath them. I'm there, too, seventy years old, wondering whether the institutions we've depended upon will withstand the strain being placed upon them. I've come to believe anyone running for political office ought to be required to pass an eighth-grade government test. I realize there might be a few constitutional problems with that requirement. And considering how little attention I paid in history class, it's quite a concession coming from me. If I could have a do-over in life—and believe me, there are quite a few things I'd like to do over—I'd pay a whole lot more attention to history. At least I had the opportunity to learn it, to ask questions, and to make up my own mind. What happens to children who grow up knowing only the chapters someone has decided are suitable for them? I don't want children taught to be ashamed of America. I want them to know what makes it worth celebrating, what we've gotten terribly wrong, and how much courage it has sometimes taken to make things right. The good, the bad, and the ugly. We don't teach history to tell children what to think. We teach it so they'll have the knowledge to think for themselves. I've spent seventy years witnessing history, much of it without fully appreciating what I was seeing. But there's something else I've come to understand: We aren't simply witnessing history. We're making it. I don't know about you, but I can't look down anymore. And I can't look away, either. Because when good people remain silent in the face of what is happening around them, eventually we're all going down.
